title: Sequence Clustering
text: silhouette plot shows well sequence fits assigned cluster. Values near 1 indicate good fit; values near 0 suggest sequence clusters; negative values indicate possible misclassification. MDS (multidimensional scaling) plot projects distance matrix 2D, showing cluster separation.
code: plot(clust, type = "silhouette") plot(clust, type = "mds")

title: Sequence Clustering
text: distance metric defines (dis)similarity sequences measured. words, quantifies different two sequences . Nestimate currently supports 9 distance metrics comparing sequences: Different metrics may produce different clustering results. need choose based research question: Hamming: compares sequences position position (best aligned sequences equal length). Edit distances (lv, osa, dl): allow insertions deletions (best sequences may shifted vary length). LCS: captures shared subsequences (best overall patterns matter exact alignment). can specify distance metric want use dissimilarity argument: distance metrics may take additional arguments. example, Hamming distance accepts temporal weighting emphasize earlier later positions:
code: # Levenshtein distance (allows insertions/deletions) clust_lv <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, dissimilarity = "lv") clust_lv$silhouette #> [1] 0.2689417  # Longest common subsequence clust_lcs <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, dissimilarity = "lcs") clust_lcs$silhouette #> [1] 0.1836091 # Emphasize earlier positions (higher lambda = faster decay) clust_weighted <- build_clusters(net,                                 k = 3,                                dissimilarity = "hamming",                                weighted = TRUE,                                lambda = 0.5) clust_weighted$silhouette #> [1] 0.2337931

title: Sequence Clustering
text: default, Nestimate uses PAM (Partitioning Around Medoids) form clusters, assigns sequence cluster represented central sequence (medoid). Besides PAM, Nestimate supports hierarchical clustering methods, build clusters step step progressively merging similar units tree-like structure (dendrogram): ward.D2 (“Ward’s Method, Squared Distances”): Minimizes increase within-cluster variance using squared distances. Typically produces compact, well-separated clusters. ward.D (“Ward’s Method”): alternative implementation Ward’s approach using different distance formulation. Similar behavior, results may vary slightly. complete (“Complete Linkage”): Defines distance clusters maximum distance members. Produces tight, compact clusters. average (“Average Linkage”): Uses average distance pairs points across clusters. Provides balance compactness flexibility. single (“Single Linkage”): Uses minimum distance points two clusters. Can capture chain-like structures may lead - loosely connected clusters. mcquitty (“McQuitty’s Method” / “WPGMA”): weighted version average linkage gives equal weight clusters regardless size. centroid (“Centroid Linkage”): Defines cluster distance based distance cluster centroids (means). Can produce intuitive groupings may introduce inconsistencies hierarchy. use methods instead PAM, need provide method argument build_clusters.
code: # Ward's method (minimizes within-cluster variance) clust_ward <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, method = "ward.D2") clust_ward$silhouette #> [1] 0.5694224  # Complete linkage clust_complete <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, method = "complete") clust_complete$silhouette #> [1] 0.8019662

title: Sequence Clustering
text: Instead clustering sequences based similar one another, can cluster together based transition dynamics. Mixture Markov models (MMM) fit separate Markov models, sequences assigned cluster whose transition structure best matches observed behavior. implement MMM, can use build_mmm(), returns net_mmm object full model details: net_mmm object contains posterior probabilities, model fit statistics (BIC, AIC, ICL), per-cluster transition matrices $models. cluster_diagnostics() works , MMM-specific columns (mixing share, average posterior probability, per-cluster classification error): posterior plot type shows distribution sequence’s max posterior probability, faceted cluster. Tight distributions near 1 indicate clean assignment; spread-distributions indicate fuzzy clusters.
code: mmm_fit <- build_mmm(net, k = 2) summary(mmm_fit) #> Mixed Markov Model #>   Sequences: 526  |  Clusters: 2  |  States: 3 #>   ICs: LL = -10074.921  |  BIC = 20256.351  |  AIC = 20183.841  |  ICL = 20536.530 #>   Quality: AvePP = 0.782  |  Entropy = 0.642  |  Class.Err = 0.0% #>  #>   Cluster  N            Mix%   AvePP #>   1        334 (63.5%)  55.7%  0.766 #>   2        192 (36.5%)  44.3%  0.808 #>  #> --- Cluster 1 (55.7%, n=334) --- #>               Directive Evaluative Metacognitive #> Directive         0.647      0.144         0.208 #> Evaluative        0.549      0.269         0.181 #> Metacognitive     0.429      0.257         0.314 #>  #> --- Cluster 2 (44.3%, n=192) --- #>               Directive Evaluative Metacognitive #> Directive         0.565      0.301         0.134 #> Evaluative        0.447      0.462         0.090 #> Metacognitive     0.398      0.435         0.166 #>   component     prior n_assigned mean_posterior     avepp #> 1         1 0.5566955        334      0.7663911 0.7663911 #> 2         2 0.4433045        192      0.8080450 0.8080450 diag_mmm <- cluster_diagnostics(mmm_fit) diag_mmm #> Cluster Diagnostics (mmm) [k = 2] #>   Sequences: 526  |  Clusters: 2  |  States: 3 #>   Quality: AvePP = 0.782  |  Entropy = 0.642  |  Class.Err = 0.0% #>   ICs: LL = -10074.921  |  BIC = 20256.351  |  AIC = 20183.841  |  ICL = 20536.530 #>  #>   Cluster  N            Mix%   AvePP  Class.Err% #>   1        334 (63.5%)  55.7%  0.766   0.0% #>   2        192 (36.5%)  44.3%  0.808   0.0% plot(diag_mmm, type = "posterior")

title: Sequence Clustering
text: sequences grouped, goal usually compare transitions behave within group. single transition network estimated sequences averages across groups hides contrast. Estimating one network per cluster preserves group’s distinct dynamics — nodes, different edge weights. result netobject_group: list netobjects sharing node set, one per cluster. Every group network supports downstream operations single netobject — plotting via plot(), resampling via bootstrap_network(), group-level edge comparison via permutation(). Two paths produce netobject_group: Manual — fit clustering build_clusters() cluster_mmm(), pass fitted clustering build_network(). Shortcut — cluster_network() collapses fitting network materialization one call either distance MMM clustering. Distance clustering groups sessions sequence similarity. Model-based MMM clustering groups Markov model best explains sequence’s transitions.

title: Network Estimation and Visualization with Nestimate + cograph
text: Nestimate unified network estimation package R. provides single entry point — build_network() — accepts sequence data, wide-format behavioral data, numeric matrices estimates networks using 10 built-methods. result netobject inherits cograph_network, every object produced Nestimate can plotted splot() directly. core design principle estimation visualization separate concerns: Nestimate handles computation (network construction, bootstrapping, permutation testing, clustering, multi-cluster analysis), cograph handles rendering. separation means analyst writes estimation code gets publication-ready figures without adapter code manual class conversion. Beyond single-network estimation, Nestimate provides complete statistical toolkit: Bootstrap stability analysis (bootstrap_network) — identifies edges survive resampling sampling artifacts. Permutation-based group comparison (permutation) — tests whether edges differ significantly conditions. Multi-cluster multi-level analysis (csum, summarize_clusters) — aggregates node-level networks cluster-level summaries hierarchical visualization. Centrality stability (centrality_stability) — assesses whether centrality rankings robust case dropping. Group-level operations — bootstrapping, permutation testing, plotting work grouped networks additional code. tutorial walks full pipeline group_regulation_long dataset shipped Nestimate.

what: Is First-Order Enough? Multi-Order Model Selection
title: Higher-Order Network Analysis with Simplicial Complexes
text: investing higher-order analysis, answer: sequential memory actually matter? Multi-Order Generative Model (MOGen; Scholtes 2017) fits Markov models increasing orders compares using information criteria. Higher-order models fit better exponentially parameters — AIC BIC find best tradeoff.  plot traces AIC BIC functions Markov order. higher-order models always fit better terms raw log-likelihood (parameter space contains lower-order one), meaningful comparison fit complexity. AIC penalises parameter 2; BIC penalises log(n), dataset much larger 2 — BIC favors small orders much aggressively AIC. Order 0: Actions independent — sequential structure. Order 1: standard Markov model sufficient. Order 2+: Higher-order dependencies exist. first-order TNA miss . Even order 1 globally optimal (BIC), specific pathways may still exhibit higher-order behavior — global model averages states. HON analysis detects local patterns. next section adds complementary, principled hypothesis test often reveals signal BIC parsimonious flag. mogen_transitions() extracts transitions given order, showing two-step contexts lead different outcomes: row second-order pathway. column two-state context, predicted next state, count empirical frequency, probability conditional P(| ). high count combined high probability predictive context: knowing previous two states pins next one. high count low probability common ambiguous context — frequent data, successor distribution spread . plot_simplicial() accepts mogen_transitions() data.frame directly. takes top pathways count renders smooth blob shared circular layout, path’s intermediate states blue target state red. Repeated states (like Specify -> Command -> Specify) get distinct positions blob covers three visually distinct nodes rather collapsing line.  zoom single frequent pathway, set max_pathways = 1 let data.frame drive selection. mogen_transitions() returns rows already sorted count, max_pathways = N always picks top N:  MOGen uses information criteria. complementary, principled approach permutation-exact LRT markov_order_test(): order kk, tests H0H_0: “process order (k−1)(k-1)” H1H_1: “process order kk” reframing conditional-independence test (k+1)(k+1)-grams. null distribution built shuffling successor labels within context — test exact H0H_0, plug-MLE bias sparse (k+1)(k+1)-gram tables.  output reveals tension hidden single criterion. BIC selects smallest order (heavy parsimony penalty). AIC permutation LRT flag higher orders significantly better — every increase order yields G2G^2 statistic far tail within-context permutation null. right panel makes concrete: grey density null G2G^2 distribution per order, colored vertical line observed value. line sits right tail, H0H_0 rejected higher order carries genuine information beyond previous one. takeaway: sequential memory exists dataset. BIC penalises parameter space order 3 enormous (4,706 degrees freedom order-3 test alone), data pay cost. Order-selection answers global question. Transition entropy answers per-state question: predictable state’s next move? transition_entropy() computes Shannon row-entropy H(P[, ]) = -sum_j P[,j] log P[,j] every state, chain-level entropy rate h(P) = sum_i pi_i H(P[, ]) (Shannon-McMillan-Breiman per-step uncertainty stationary distribution pi), redundancy H(pi) - h(P) (much previous state reduces uncertainty next).  bar state’s outgoing-distribution entropy bits; bar’s width proportional stationary probability, visual area sums entropy rate h(P). dashed red line marks h(P); dotted line marks ceiling log_2(n) every state uniform outgoing distribution. States whose bar pokes near ceiling unpredictable hubs (next state essentially random); short bars deterministic — arrive , next step largely fixed.

what: The entropy of a transition network
title: Transition Matrix Entropy
text: transition_entropy() accepts fitted network, transition matrix, sequence data. call computes entropy rate HH, stationary entropy H(π)H(\pi) (ceiling apply consecutive actions independent), difference, redundancy. process runs 2.41 bits per step ceiling log⁡29=3.17\log_2 9 = 3.17; normalized entropy 0.76 scale-free version Krejtz et al. (2025) report. Regulation far scripted, knowing current action removes 22% uncertainty next one (relative redundancy 0.22): sequence carries real information, empirical justification modeling transitions rather activity frequencies alone.
code: net <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "relative",                      actor = "Actor", action = "Action", time = "Time") te <- transition_entropy(net) te #> Transition Entropy (9 states, bits; ceiling = 3.170) #>  #>                           raw            normalised #>   Entropy rate    h(P)  = 2.409 bits    0.760 #>   Stationary    H(pi)  = 2.782 bits    0.878 #>   Redundancy   H(pi)-h = 0.373 bits    0.134 #>  #> Normalised: h(P) and H(pi) are raw / log_2(n_states) (0 = deterministic, 1 = uniform); #>   redundancy is the relative redundancy (H(pi) - h(P)) / H(pi), not raw / log_2(n_states).

Sliding window across transition stream — design Krejtz et al. (2025), use 30-second windows gaze transitions — turns entropy process measure. entropy_trajectory() builds transitions within actor’s sequence, orders time, computes one entropy value per window.  faint line one 500-transition window stepped 100; bold curve loess trend per achievement group. title: Network Estimation and Analysis with Nestimate
text: Psychological network analysis estimates conditional dependency structure among set variables. Variables (e.g., symptoms, traits, behaviors) represented nodes, edges represent partial correlations — association two variables controlling others. approach reveals variables directly connected versus whose association mediated variables (Saqr et al., 2024). Nestimate supports three estimation methods psychological networks, accessed build_network() interface: Correlation networks (method = "cor") estimate pairwise Pearson correlations produce fully connected undirected networks. informative starting point, distinguish direct indirect associations. Partial correlation networks (method = "pcor") control variables, revealing direct associations. provide accurate picture dependency structure, though results can noisy small samples. Regularized networks via EBICglasso (method = "glasso") apply L1 regularization precision matrix, shrinking weak unreliable edges exactly zero. recommended approach psychological network analysis, balances model fit complexity produces sparse, interpretable, replicable structures.

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: wtna() builds networks binary (one-hot) data using temporal windows — directed transitions windows, undirected co-occurrence within windows, mixed network combining .
code: data(learning_activities) net_wtna  <- wtna(learning_activities, actor = "student",                   method = "transition", type = "relative") net_mixed <- wtna(learning_activities, actor = "student",                   method = "both", type = "relative")

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: cooccurrence() builds undirected co-occurrence networks 6 input formats (delimited fields, long/bipartite, binary matrix, wide sequence, lists) 8 similarity methods (Jaccard, cosine, association strength, Dice, ).
code: # From a long-format data frame net_co <- cooccurrence(human_long, field = "action", by = "session_id",                        similarity = "jaccard", threshold = 0.1)

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: implemented scratch dependency igraph, qgraph, bootnet.
code: data(srl_strategies) net_gl  <- build_network(srl_strategies, method = "glasso") net_mgm <- build_network(mixed_data, method = "mgm")   # scales + demographics  predictability(net_gl)   # R-squared per node from network structure

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_mlvar() estimates three networks simultaneously ESM/EMA diary data — three pillars mlVAR analysis single function call: Temporal (directed) — lagged fixed effects: predicts across time Contemporaneous (undirected) — partial correlations within-person residuals: moves together right now -subjects (undirected) — partial correlations person means: differs Machine-precision equivalence mlVAR::mlVAR() validated across 25 real ESM datasets, runs 1.45× faster.
code: data(chatgpt_srl) fit <- build_mlvar(chatgpt_srl, vars = c("planning", "monitoring", "evaluation"),                    id = "id", day = "day", beep = "beep")  fit$temporal          # directed network of lagged effects fit$contemporaneous   # undirected within-person partial correlations fit$between           # undirected between-persons partial correlations coefs(fit)            # tidy data.frame: beta, SE, t, p, CI for every edge

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_gimme() estimates separate network person using Group Iterative Mean Estimation (GIMME) algorithm, aggregates group-level picture. Use -person heterogeneity matters single group network average meaningfully different individuals.
code: fit_g <- build_gimme(panel_data, vars = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), id = "id") fit_g$group_network       # aggregated group-level paths fit_g$individual_networks # one network per person

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_clusters() partitions sequences k groups using pairwise distance matrices. Supports 9 distance metrics 8 clustering algorithms. build_clusters() build_mmm() results pass directly build_network().
code: clust <- build_clusters(net, k = 3, dissimilarity = "hamming", method = "ward.D2") plot(clust, type = "silhouette") cluster_nets <- build_network(clust, method = "tna")

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_mmm() discovers latent subgroups sequences share similar transition dynamics via EM — without pre-labelling groups. BIC/AIC/ICL model selection via compare_mmm().
code: mmm   <- build_mmm(net, k = 3) compare_mmm(net, k = 2:6)   # model selection plot + table mmm_nets <- build_network(mmm, method = "tna")

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: build_mcml() decomposes network macro (-cluster) micro (within-cluster) layers nodes belong known groups.
code: clusters <- list(Metacognitive = c("Planning", "Monitoring"),                  Cognitive     = c("Elaboration", "Organisation")) mcml <- cluster_summary(net, clusters) mcml$macro$weights

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: Capture dependencies beyond first-order transitions:
code: hon  <- build_hon(net, max_order = 2) pathways(hon)                      # arrow-notation path strings hypa <- build_hypa(net) hypa$over                          # over-represented paths with p-values

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: Go beyond edges — find cliques, holes, high-order connectivity using tools algebraic topology.
code: sc <- build_simplicial(net, method = "clique") betti_numbers(sc)          # connected components, cycles, voids euler_characteristic(sc) ph <- persistent_homology(net)  # track topology across thresholds plot(ph) qa <- q_analysis(sc)       # Atkin's Q-connectivity structure vectors

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: Visualize raw sequence data index plots state distribution charts — clustering.
code: # Sequence index plot: one row per person, coloured by state sequence_plot(net)  # After clustering: faceted by cluster clust <- build_clusters(net, k = 3) sequence_plot(clust, type = "index")  # State distribution over time distribution_plot(net, type = "area") distribution_plot(clust, type = "bar")

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: sequence_compare() extracts k-gram patterns grouped sequences, counts per-group frequencies, tests statistical differences via permutation — answering question “groups actually behave differently, ?”
code: data(human_long) net <- build_network(human_long, method = "tna",                      action = "action", actor = "session_id",                      time = "time", group = "phase")  res <- sequence_compare(net, sub = 2:4, test = "chisq", adjust = "fdr") res$patterns                        # per-pattern frequencies + p-values plot(res)                           # back-to-back pyramid chart plot(res, style = "heatmap")        # heatmap for many patterns

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: association_rules() mines “B” patterns sequences binary matrices using Apriori algorithm. Returns support, confidence, lift, conviction every rule threshold.
code: rules <- association_rules(net, min_support = 0.05, min_confidence = 0.6) rules$rules                       # tidy data.frame, sorted by lift pathways(rules)                   # rules as arrow-notation strings  # From a raw binary matrix rules2 <- association_rules(binary_mat, min_support = 0.1)

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: predict_links() scores unobserved node pairs using structural similarity, identifying missing connections likely exist. evaluate_links() computes AUC, precision, recall held-edges.
code: preds <- predict_links(net)       # common neighbours, Adamic-Adar, Katz, ... head(preds$scores)                # sorted by predicted score  # Evaluate against known missing edges eval  <- evaluate_links(net, held_out = test_edges) eval$auc

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: markov_stability() measures stable network partition random-walk dynamics different time scales — resolution-free way find communities. passage_time() computes expected first-passage return times states.
code: stab <- markov_stability(net, times = seq(0.1, 10, 0.1)) plot(stab)                # stability vs time-scale curve  pt <- passage_time(net) pt$first_passage          # expected steps to reach state j from state i pt$return_time            # expected steps to return to the same state

title: Dynamic, Probabilistic, and Higher-Order Network Analysis
text: Every network type shares validation pipeline.
code: # Bootstrap confidence intervals boot <- bootstrap_network(net, iter = 1000) summary(boot)  # Permutation test: are two networks different? perm <- permutation(group_nets$`Cluster 1`, group_nets$`Cluster 2`)  # Network Comparison Test (NCT): formal test of structure + global strength nct_res <- nct(data1, data2, iter = 500) print(nct_res)            # M-statistic, S-statistic, per-edge p-values  # Split-half reliability network_reliability(net)  # Centrality stability (CS-coefficient) centrality_stability(net)  # Glasso-specific bootstrap (edge inclusion + centrality CIs) boot_gl <- boot_glasso(net_pna, iter = 1000)

title: Bayesian Dirichlet-Multinomial comparison of two transition networks — bayes_compare
text: Compares two transition networks estimated build_network (method "relative" "frequency") using Bayesian Dirichlet-Multinomial model. outgoing transitions source state modelled Multinomial draw Dirichlet prior transition probabilities. Jeffreys prior posterior transitions state \(\) \(\mathrm{Dirichlet}(c_i + \alpha)\), \(c_i\) observed outgoing counts. edge probability marginally Beta-distributed, posterior mean difference two networks available closed form credible interval obtained Monte Carlo. complement permutation: permutation test answers "difference extreme chance?"; Bayesian comparison answers "plausible range true difference, precisely estimated given counts?". edge outgoing transitions source state yields wide credible interval even row-normalised probability looks decisive. bayes_compare() also accepts two net_edge_betweenness objects (source method "relative" ). Edge betweenness nonlinear function whole transition matrix, instead Beta marginals full transition matrix drawn group's row-wise Dirichlet posterior edge betweenness recomputed every draw - Bayesian analogue permutation()'s edge-betweenness dispatch. result summarises posterior EB(x) - EB(y): diff posterior mean difference, prob_x/prob_y hold posterior mean betweenness matrices, observed_diff plug-difference two input networks. inputs must use invert setting.

code: # A three-variable ESM panel: 20 people x 20 beeps. `tired` is driven by # `happy` one beep earlier, so the temporal network should recover it. if (requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)) {   set.seed(1)   n_beep <- 20   ar1 <- function(n, phi) as.numeric(stats::filter(stats::rnorm(n), phi,                                                    method = "recursive"))   panel <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(20), function(i) {     happy <- ar1(n_beep, 0.4)     data.frame(       id    = i,       beep  = seq_len(n_beep),       happy = happy + stats::rnorm(1),       calm  = ar1(n_beep, 0.3) + stats::rnorm(1),       tired = 0.5 * c(0, happy[-n_beep]) + stats::rnorm(n_beep) +               stats::rnorm(1)     )   }))   fit <- build_mlvar(panel, vars = c("happy", "calm", "tired"),                      id = "id", beep = "beep")   fit   coefs(fit)   summary(fit) } #>           network n_nodes n_edges density mean_abs_weight n_positive n_negative #> 1        temporal       3       6       1      0.11569402          2          4 #> 2 contemporaneous       3       3       1      0.05304465          1          2 #> 3         between       3       3       1      0.15389239          2          1

title: Build a Simplicial Complex — build_simplicial
text: Constructs simplicial complex network higher-order pathway object. Two construction methods available: Clique complex ("clique"): every clique thresholded non-zero graph becomes simplex. Edges absolute weight \(\geq\) threshold retained. standard bridge graph theory algebraic topology. Pathway complex ("pathway"): higher-order pathway net_hon net_hypa becomes simplex. type = "vr" (alias "rips"), input treated non-negative distance / dissimilarity matrix Vietoris-Rips filtration constructed: k-simplex \(\sigma\) enters \(\max_{(,j) \\sigma} d(,j)\). Use max_scale cap filtration diameter; edges d(,j) > max_scale excluded. Filtration values attached $filtration returned object persistent_homology() can read directly.

title: Clique expansion of a hypergraph — clique_expansion
text: clique expansion standard "loss-y lossless--pairwise" projection: preserves pairs co-occurred often discards higher-order grouping. Comparing clique_expansion(hg) directly-estimated pairwise network (e.g. via cooccurrence() data) quantifies much information carried hyperedge structure. Computed one BLAS call via tcrossprod(incidence); runs O(n_nodes^2 * n_hyperedges) time, fast typical sizes. Closes /O cycle: event data -> bipartite_groups() -> clique_expansion() -> function accepts netobject (centrality, bootstrap, clustering, plotting via cograph).

title: Cluster Choice – sweep k, dissimilarity and method — cluster_choice
text: Type cheat-sheet: "auto" Default. Picks one others based axes swept. k--> "lines"; one categorical axis swept -> "bars"; k plus one categorical -> "lines"; k plus two categoricals -> "facet"; categoricals without k -> "heatmap". "lines" Silhouette across k (mean_within_dist k swept axis), one line per non-k axis present. "bars" Horizontal bar chart silhouette per axis level. Bars sorted silhouette. "heatmap" Tiled silhouette across two categorical axes. Requires dissimilarity method swept. "tradeoff" Scatter: silhouette (y) vs size_ratio (x). Works sweep; labels point. "facet" Lines vs k, colour one categorical axis, facet another. Requires k plus two categoricals. Asking type data support raises error pointing alternatives.

title: Cluster Summary Statistics — cluster_summary
text: x Network input. Accepts multiple formats: matrix Numeric adjacency/weight matrix. Row column names used node labels. Values represent edge weights (e.g., transition counts, co-occurrence frequencies, probabilities). netobject network object built build_network. weight matrix x$weights aggregated; bare cograph_network coerced netobject first. tna tna object tna package. Extracts x$weights. mcml mcml object returned unchanged. clusters Cluster/group assignments nodes. Accepts multiple formats: NULL (default) usable : clusters required NULL raises error. Auto-detection cluster column netobject's node table happens build_mcml, calls function detected assignment. vector Cluster membership node, order matrix rows/columns. Can numeric (1, 2, 3) character ("", "B"). Cluster names derived unique values. Example: c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3) assigns first two nodes cluster 1. data.frame data frame first column contains node names second column contains group/cluster names. Example: data.frame(node = c("", "B", "C"), group = c("G1", "G1", "G2")) named list Explicit mapping cluster names node labels. List names become cluster names, values character vectors node labels must match matrix row/column names. Example: list(Alpha = c("", "B"), Beta = c("C", "D")) method Aggregation method combining edge weights within/clusters. Controls multiple node--node edges summarized: "sum" (default) Sum edge weights. Best count data (e.g., transition frequencies). Preserves total flow. "mean" Average edge weight. Best cluster sizes differ want control size. Note: input already transition matrix (rows sum 1), "mean" avoids size bias. Example: cluster 5 nodes 5x weight cluster 1 node. "median" Median edge weight. Robust outliers. "max" Maximum edge weight. Captures strongest connection. "min" Minimum edge weight. Captures weakest connection. "density" Sum (non-zero) edge weights divided number possible edges two clusters (n_i * n_j). Normalizes cluster size combinations. zero/NA edges stripped aggregation, equals "mean" exactly cluster-pair block fully dense (zero edges), strictly smaller "mean" zero edges present (divides larger possible-edge count). "geomean" Geometric mean positive weights. Useful multiplicative processes. directed Logical. TRUE (default), treat network directed. ->B B->separate edges. FALSE, edges undirected matrix symmetrized processing. compute_within Logical. TRUE (default), compute within-cluster transition matrices cluster. cluster gets n_i x n_i matrix showing internal node--node transitions. Set FALSE skip computation better performance -cluster summary needed.

code: # A three-variable ESM panel: 20 people x 20 beeps. `tired` is driven by # `happy` one beep earlier, so the temporal network should recover it. if (requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)) {   set.seed(1)   n_beep <- 20   ar1 <- function(n, phi) as.numeric(stats::filter(stats::rnorm(n), phi,                                                    method = "recursive"))   panel <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(20), function(i) {     happy <- ar1(n_beep, 0.4)     data.frame(       id    = i,       beep  = seq_len(n_beep),       happy = happy + stats::rnorm(1),       calm  = ar1(n_beep, 0.3) + stats::rnorm(1),       tired = 0.5 * c(0, happy[-n_beep]) + stats::rnorm(n_beep) +               stats::rnorm(1)     )   }))   fit <- build_mlvar(panel, vars = c("happy", "calm", "tired"),                      id = "id", beep = "beep")   fit   coefs(fit)   summary(fit) } #>           network n_nodes n_edges density mean_abs_weight n_positive n_negative #> 1        temporal       3       6       1      0.11569402          2          4 #> 2 contemporaneous       3       3       1      0.05304465          1          2 #> 3         between       3       3       1      0.15389239          2          1

title: Compare two networks descriptively — compare_model
text: Computes battery descriptive comparison metrics two networks two weight matrices: weight deviations (mean / median / RMS / max absolute difference, relative mean absolute difference, coefficient-- variation ratio), four correlation measures (Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, distance correlation), five dissimilarity measures (Euclidean, Manhattan, Canberra, Bray-Curtis, Frobenius), five similarity measures (Cosine, Jaccard, Dice, Overlap, RV), pattern agreements, side--side network metrics. Ignored. plot.net_comparison() print.net_comparison(): Ignored. y netobject, cograph_network, numeric square matrix. scaling Scaling applied weight matrices comparison. One : "none" Identity (default). "minmax" \((w - \min) / (\max - \min)\); maps \([0, 1]\). "max" \(w / \max(|w|)\); preserves sign. "rank" Min-max average ranks; ordinal scaling. "zscore" \((w - \bar w) / s_w\); standard score. "robust" \((w - \mathrm{med}(w)) / \mathrm{mad}(w)\); Huber-style robust z-score, resists outliers. "log" \(\log(w)\); requires \(w > 0\). "log1p" \(\log(1 + w)\); admits \(w \ge 0\). "softmax" Numerically stable softmax flattened vector. "quantile" Empirical CDF flattened vector. "frobenius" Divide matrix Frobenius norm \(\|W\|_F = \sqrt{\sum w_{ij}^2}\); matrix-level normalisation. "row" Row-stochastic normalisation (row's absolute values sum 1). meaningful non-negative matrices; rows summing zero left unchanged. Scalings produce negative weights (zscore, robust) compatible network = TRUE side--side metrics use Nestimate's base-R Floyd-Warshall, handles negative weights. measures Character vector centrality measures compare. Empty default (centrality block). built-measure valid: "OutStrength", "InStrength", "ClosenessIn", "ClosenessOut", "Closeness", "Betweenness", "BetweennessRSP", "Diffusion", "Clustering", "InCloseness", "OutCloseness". Unknown names ignored warning. network Logical. Include side--side network metrics summary()? Default TRUE. , j netobject_group: index name two member networks compare. One "scatter" (default - edge-weight scatter OLS fit correlation overlay), "heatmap" (n n grid x - y differences using diverging palette), "diff_hist" (histogram |x - y| absolute differences rug + density), "weight_dist" (overlaid distributions |x| |y| edge weights), "" (2 2 grid four panels; requires gridExtra package). combined type = "" combined = TRUE (default), four panels stitched 2x2 gtable. "bootstrap" (via vertex_compare()) appends structural rows (density, mean weight, centralization, reciprocity) global boot_se, boot_ci_lower, boot_ci_upper, boot_z, boot_p, boot_sig. title: Build a Co-occurrence Network — cooccurrence
text: Constructs undirected co-occurrence network various input formats. Entities appear together transaction, document, record connected, edge weights reflecting raw counts similarity measure. Argument names follow citenets convention.

title: Build a Co-occurrence Network — cooccurrence
code: cooccurrence(   data,   field = NULL,   by = NULL,   sep = NULL,   similarity = c("none", "jaccard", "cosine", "inclusion", "association", "dice",     "equivalence", "relative"),   threshold = 0,   min_occur = 1L,   diagonal = TRUE,   top_n = NULL,   ... )

title: Build a Co-occurrence Network — cooccurrence
text: data Input data. Accepts: data.frame delimited column (field + sep). data.frame long/bipartite format (field + ). binary (0/1) data.frame matrix (auto-detected). wide sequence data.frame matrix (non-binary). list character vectors (element transaction). field Character. entity column - determines nodes . delimited format, single column whose values split sep. long/bipartite format, item column. multi-column delimited, vector column names whose split values pooled per row. Character NULL. links nodes. long/bipartite format, grouping column (e.g., "paper_id", "session_id"). unique value defines one transaction. NULL (default), entities co-occur within row/document. sep Character NULL. Separator splitting delimited fields (e.g., ";", ","). Default NULL. similarity Character. Similarity measure applied raw co-occurrence counts. One : "none" Raw co-occurrence counts. "jaccard" \(C_{ij} / (f_i + f_j - C_{ij})\). "cosine" \(C_{ij} / \sqrt{f_i \cdot f_j}\) (Salton's cosine). "inclusion" \(C_{ij} / \min(f_i, f_j)\) (Simpson coefficient). "association" \(C_{ij} / (f_i \cdot f_j)\) (association strength / probabilistic affinity index; van Eck & Waltman, 2009). "dice" \(2 C_{ij} / (f_i + f_j)\). "equivalence" \(C_{ij}^2 / (f_i \cdot f_j)\) (Salton's cosine squared). "relative" Row-normalized: row sums 1. threshold Numeric. Minimum edge weight retain. Edges value set zero. Applied similarity normalization. Default 0. min_occur Integer. Minimum entity frequency (number transactions entity must appear ). Entities threshold dropped computing co-occurrence. Default 1 (keep ). diagonal Logical. TRUE (default), diagonal co-occurrence matrix kept (item self-co-occurrence = item frequency). FALSE, diagonal zeroed. top_n Integer NULL. specified, return top top_n edges weight. Default NULL (edges). ... Currently unused.

title: Build a Co-occurrence Network — cooccurrence
text: netobject (undirected, class c("netobject", "cograph_network")) method = "co_occurrence_fn" $data = NULL - function go build_network, result carries source data data-resampling verbs (bootstrap_network, permutation) run . $weights matrix holds similarity (raw) co-occurrence values, one row/column per retained item. $params list records similarity, threshold, min_occur, diagonal, top_n, n_transactions n_items.

title: Build a Co-occurrence Network — cooccurrence
text: Six input formats supported, auto-detected combination field, , sep: Delimited: field + sep (single column). cell split sep, trimmed, de-duplicated per row. Multi-column delimited: field (vector) + sep. Values multiple columns split, pooled, de-duplicated per row. Long bipartite: field + . Groups ; unique values field within group form transaction. Binary matrix: field//sep, values 0/1. Columns items, rows transactions. Wide sequence: field//sep, non-binary. Unique values across row form transaction. List: plain list character vectors. pipeline converts formats list character vectors (transactions), optionally filters min_occur, builds binary transaction matrix, computes crossprod(B) raw co-occurrence counts, normalizes via chosen similarity, applies threshold top_n filtering.

title: Build a Co-occurrence Network — cooccurrence
text: van Eck, N. J., & Waltman, L. (2009). normalize co-occurrence data? analysis well-known similarity measures. Journal American Society Information Science Technology, 60(8), 1635–1651.

title: Build a Co-occurrence Network — cooccurrence
code: # Delimited field (e.g., keyword co-occurrence) df <- data.frame(   id = 1:4,   keywords = c("network; graph", "graph; matrix; network",                "matrix; algebra", "network; algebra; graph") ) net <- cooccurrence(df, field = "keywords", sep = ";")  # Long/bipartite long_df <- data.frame(   paper = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3),   keyword = c("network", "graph", "matrix", "graph", "algebra",               "network", "algebra") ) net <- cooccurrence(long_df, field = "keyword", by = "paper")  # List of transactions transactions <- list(c("A", "B"), c("B", "C"), c("A", "B", "C")) net <- cooccurrence(transactions, similarity = "jaccard")  # Binary matrix bin <- matrix(c(1,0,1, 1,1,0, 0,1,1), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,               dimnames = list(NULL, c("X", "Y", "Z"))) net <- cooccurrence(bin)

title: Transition Entropy Network — entropy_network
text: x netobject, cograph_network, tna object, row-stochastic numeric transition matrix, wide sequence data.frame (rows = actors, columns = time-steps; relative transition network built automatically). base Numeric. Logarithm base. 2 (default) bits, exp(1) nats, 10 hartleys. weight Character. Edge weight definition: "contribution" (default) \(\pi_i P_{ij} \log_b(1/P_{ij})\) - edge's additive share entropy rate; edge weights sum exactly \(h(P)\). Thick edges transitions frequent unpredictable. "surprisal" \(\log_b(1/P_{ij})\) - information content observing transition, ignoring often occurs. Thick edges rare, surprising transitions. Low surprisal = expected transition; edge-level predictability reading. "production" \(F_{ij} \log_b(F_{ij}/F_{ji})\) \(F_{ij} = \pi_i P_{ij}\) - edge's contribution entropy production rate (irreversibility). Positive dominant direction pair, negative reverse; two always sum \((F_{ij}-F_{ji}) \log_b(F_{ij}/F_{ji}) \ge 0\). Pairs flow one direction infinite production excluded (weight 0); count reported $params$n_oneway_pairs. Total included pairs $params$production_rate - 0 iff chain reversible (detailed balance). scaling Character. "none" (default) keeps weights base-units. "share" (contribution ) expresses edge percentage entropy rate - weights sum 100 label reads "transition holds x% process's unpredictability"; comparable across networks regardless state count base. "chance" (surprisal ) divides \(\log_b n\) - surprisal chance-level transition \(n\) next states equally likely: 1 = chance level, 1 = expected transition, 1 = rarer chance. normalize Logical. TRUE (default), rows sum 1 normalised automatically (warning).

Clique-motif eigenvector centrality (CEC): forms clique-expanded pairwise graph \(W\) \(W_{ij} = |\{e : , j \e\}|\) returns leading eigenvector \(W\). Equivalent running igraph::eigen_centrality() clique_expansion() output. Z-eigenvector centrality (ZEC): solves linear eigen-equation hyperedge tensor, $$\lambda\, x_i \;=\; \sum_{e 
i }\; \prod_{j \e,\; j 
eq } x_j,$$ via power iteration. Works hypergraphs mixed edge sizes. H-eigenvector centrality (HEC): solves power-k-1 eigen-equation, $$\lambda\, x_i^{k-1} \;=\; \sum_{e 
i }\; \prod_{j \e,\; j 
eq } x_j.$$ uniform hypergraphs (hyperedges size \(k\)), equivalent normalizing ZEC update geometric-mean exponent \(1/(k-1)\). mixed sizes, effective exponent taken largest hyperedge; expect slightly different rankings ZEC mixed case.

title: Hypergraph eigenvector centralities — hypergraph_centrality
text: "clique" (CEC) variant validated igraph::eigen_centrality (cosine ~ 1). "Z" "H" variants (experimental) - validated clean-room list-based tensor power iteration (operator, different loop structure); R package exposes tensor eigenvectors primitive independent comparison.

title: Normalized hypergraph Laplacian — hypergraph_laplacian
text: Computes normalized Laplacian hypergraph, either classic Zhou-Huang-Scholkopf form binary incidence pattern (type = "zhou") random-walk form edge-dependent vertex weights (type = "random_walk"), weighted incidence cells (e.g. summed weights produced bipartite_groups()) determine random walker lands inside hyperedge, resulting non-reversible walk symmetrized stationary distribution (Chung 2005). Laplacians symmetric positive semi-definite eigenvalues [0, 2]; binary incidence unit hyperedge weights coincide.

title: Structural measures for a hypergraph — hypergraph_measures
text: object class hypergraph_measures (named list) components: Node-level (length n_nodes)  hyperdegree Number hyperedges containing node. node_strength Total participation: node \(\), \(\sum_{e \ni } |e|\). node many large hyperedges high strength. max_edge_size Size largest hyperedge containing node. co_degree n_nodes x n_nodes matrix: co_degree[, j] = |{e : , j e}| (number hyperedges co-containing nodes \(\) \(j\)). Diagonal zero. Hyperedge-level (length n_hyperedges m x m)  edge_sizes Hyperedge sizes \(|e|\). edge_pairwise_overlap m x m matrix: |e_i intersect e_j|. Diagonal zero. overlap_coefficient m x m: |e_i e_j| / min(|e_i|, |e_j|). Measures much smaller hyperedge contained larger. jaccard m x m: symmetric overlap index |e_i e_j| / |e_i union e_j|. Global (scalars)  density k-uniform hypergraphs: m / choose(n, k). mixed sizes: sum(|e|) / (n * m) (mean fraction nodes per hyperedge). avg_edge_size Mean edge_sizes. size_distribution Tabulation hyperedge sizes (passed hg). intersection_profile Distribution pairwise hyperedge intersection sizes - useful spotting whether hyperedges overlap mostly trivially share substantial cores (et al. 2020). pairwise_participation Fraction node pairs co-appearing least one hyperedge. n_nodes, n_hyperedges Convenience scalars. print.hypergraph_measures(): input x invisibly.

title: Structural measures for a hypergraph — hypergraph_measures
text: measures computed via standard matrix operations binary incidence \(B = (b_{ij})\) \(b_{ij} = 1\) iff node \(\) hyperedge \(j\): hyperdegree = rowSums(B), edge_sizes = colSums(B) co_degree = tcrossprod(B) (zero diagonal) edge_pairwise_overlap = crossprod(B) (zero diagonal) overlap_coefficient[, j] = overlap[, j] / min(edge_sizes[], edge_sizes[j]) jaccard[, j] = overlap[, j] / (edge_sizes[] + edge_sizes[j] - overlap[, j]) Empty hypergraph (n_hyperedges == 0) returns trivial zeros empty matrices.

what: Magnitude difference between the frequency and probability views — magnitude_difference
title: Magnitude difference between the frequency and probability views — magnitude_difference
text: Quantifies, per edge, much row-normalization moves transition network two natural summaries: raw transition counts (frequency / FTNA, build_network(method = "frequency")) row-conditional probabilities (TNA, build_network(method = "relative")). two matrices rank edges differently - edge large counts can modest probability, rare-source edge can dominate row probability. per-edge discrepancy common scale magnitude difference.

title: Magnitude difference between the frequency and probability views — magnitude_difference
code: magnitude_difference(   data,   actor = "Actor",   action = "Action",   time = NULL,   metric = c("abs_diff", "chord_dist", "atanh_diff", "geom_norm_diff", "cv_inflation"),   scale = c("tna_range", "rank_minmax", "minmax", "none"),   format = c("auto", "long", "wide") )  # S3 method for class 'magnitude_difference' print(x, ...)  # S3 method for class 'magnitude_difference' plot(x, type = c("stacked", "circular"), min_show = 0.01, title = NULL, ...)

title: Magnitude difference between the frequency and probability views — magnitude_difference
text: data Long- wide-format event log (data.frame). actor, action, time Column names data (long format). time may NULL. metric Discrepancy metric. One "abs_diff" (default; absolute difference, simplest robust), "chord_dist" (chord distance unit sphere), "atanh_diff" (Fisher z-style bounded scale), "geom_norm_diff" (geometric-mean normalized; amplifies small edges), "cv_inflation" (per-vector SD-standardized absolute difference). scale two weight matrices placed common scale differencing. "tna_range" (default) rescales FTNA linearly TNA's [min, max] range leaves TNA untouched, difference TNA probability units. "rank_minmax" converts matrix's values ranks scaled [0, 1] (ordinal). "minmax" scales matrix's raw values [0, 1] separately (asymmetric - TNA's max FTNA's max map value despite differing native ranges). "none" uses raw weights. format Input format passed build_network(); "auto" (default) treats data wide action column. x print() plot() methods: object class magnitude_difference. ... plot.magnitude_difference(): Ignored. print.magnitude_difference(): Passed plotting helpers (ignored print). type Plot style, "stacked" (default) "circular". min_show type = "circular", drop edges whose magnitude fraction maximum. title Plot title. NULL generates one metric scale.

what: Test the Markov order of a sequential process — markov_order_test
title: Test the Markov order of a sequential process — markov_order_test
text: Principled test whether categorical sequence best described \(k\)-th order Markov chain. order \(k = 1, \ldots,\) max_order, function computes classical likelihood-ratio statistic (\(G^2\)) conditional independence \(s \perp x \mid w\), \(w\) \((k-1)\)-gram context, \(x\) extra (k-th-back) state added order \(k\), \(s\) next state. \(H_0\) (order-\((k-1)\) correct), \(s\) independent \(x\) given \(w\). null distribution obtained exact within-\(w\) permutation test: context \(w\) successor labels exchangeable \(H_0\), shuffling \(s\) within \(w\)-group yields exact reference distribution \(G^2\). plug-MLE bias refitting per replicate. asymptotic \(\chi^2\) p-value reported alongside reference. Order selection sequential: order raised test rejects, stops first non-rejection. reported optimal_order therefore highest \(k\) whose test - every test - rejected level alpha, .e. one first non-rejection; 0 order 1 already rejected, max_order test accepts.

title: Test the Markov order of a sequential process — markov_order_test
code: markov_order_test(   data,   max_order = 3L,   n_perm = 500L,   alpha = 0.05,   parallel = FALSE,   n_cores = 2L,   seed = NULL )  # S3 method for class 'net_markov_order' print(x, ...)  # S3 method for class 'net_markov_order_group' print(x, ...)  # S3 method for class 'net_markov_order' summary(object, ...)  # S3 method for class 'net_markov_order' plot(x, panel = c("both", "ic", "permutation"), combined = TRUE, ...)

title: Two-variable mosaic analysis (chi-square test + flat mosaic) — mosaic_analysis
text: Analyses association two categorical columns data.frame. Builds contingency table, drops sparse categories min_count, runs Pearson chi-square test (Fisher's exact test), computes Cramer's V df-adjusted effect-size label, draws flat ggplot2 mosaic whose tile area encodes counts whose fill encodes standardized Pearson residual (Nestimate diverging palette). tabular output tidy one-row-per-cell data.frame.

text: x One four data-bearing Nestimate classes: netobject (single mosaic $weights), netobject_group (one panel per group), mcml (-cluster mosaic default; per-cluster panels level = "within"), htna (single mosaic $weights; htna inherits netobject geometry matches). Also accepts contingency table plain numeric matrix ad-hoc plotting. ... Flat styling overrides forwarded flat renderer style = "flat" (otherwise ignored). xlab, ylab Axis labels. NULL (default) draws axis title four data-bearing methods; table / matrix methods default "Row" "Column". Pass string set one. range Numeric length 2 giving lower upper colour-scale limits standardized residual. NULL (default) auto-fits limits symmetric range c(-M, M) M = max(|stdres|) floored 1, signal squished legend stays readable near-independent table. Pass explicit range (e.g. c(-4, 4) tna-style display, c(-6, 6) moderate clipping) clamp colour scale. top_angle, left_angle Rotation degrees top (x) left (y) tick labels. NULL (default) uses auto rule 90 n_levels > 3 else 0 axis. Pass numeric override (e.g. top_angle = 45, left_angle = 0). residuals One "permutation" (default) "asymptotic". "permutation" computes empirical-null z-scores shuffling one variable's labels n_perm draws reporting (O - mean_perm) / sd_perm per cell. Robust sparse tables. "asymptotic" returns stats::chisq.test()$stdres (closed-form (O - E) / sqrt(E*(1 - p_row)*(1 - p_col)) vcd tna use). n_perm Number permutations residuals = "permutation". Default 500; use >= 1000 stable tail estimates. seed Optional integer seed permutation RNG. Use reproducible plots; ignored residuals = "asymptotic". values Logical. TRUE, overlay cell's standardized residual numeric label (one decimal). Text colour switches white saturated cells (|stdres| > 1.5) dark grey otherwise. Default FALSE – colour bar legend already conveys sign magnitude. style Character. "macro" (default) draws single mosaic x$macro$weights (cluster--cluster aggregate); "clusters" draws one mosaic per cluster x$clusters[[k]]$weights, faceted one combined ggplot. ncol Number columns multi-panel layout. title: Mosaic Plot of a Network's Transition or Co-occurrence Counts — mosaic_plot
text: Column widths proportional row marginals weight matrix (incoming totals matrix transposed, transitions). Within column, segment heights proportional row's conditional distribution. Cell fill standardized residual independence null – permutation z-score default, closed-form stats::chisq.test() residual residuals = "asymptotic" (see residuals) – diverging palette whose limits auto-fit observed residuals unless range supplied. Mosaics need integer counts: $weights already integer (method = "frequency" / "co_occurrence") used directly; single netobject / htna otherwise (relative, glasso, cor, ...) order-1 transition counts recounted raw $data sequences. function errors neither integer weights $data available.

title: Network Comparison Test — nct
text: Tests whether two networks estimated independent samples differ three levels: global strength (M-statistic), network structure (S-statistic, max absolute edge difference), individual edges (E-statistic per edge). Inference via permutation group labels.

title: Mean First Passage Times — passage_time
text: Uses Kemeny-Snell fundamental matrix formula: $$M_{ij} = \frac{Z_{jj} - Z_{ij}}{\pi_j}, \quad       Z = (- P + \Pi)^{-1}$$ \(\Pi_{ij} = \pi_j\). Requires ergodic (irreducible, aperiodic) chain.

title: Persistent Homology — persistent_homology
text: Computes persistent homology via full boundary-matrix reduction \(\mathbb{Z}/2\) (Edelsbrunner, Letscher & Zomorodian 2000). returned persistence diagram pairs k-dimensional homology class simplex whose addition creates (birth) simplex whose addition destroys (death). Essential classes - never killed - reported death = 0 clique mode (similarity scale, descending) death = Inf VR mode (distance scale, ascending). Two filtration modes supported: type = "clique" Weighted clique filtration. Input treated similarity matrix; high-weight simplices appear early. k-simplex \(\sigma\), filtration value \(\min_{(,j) \\sigma}\,|w(,j)|\). Thresholds run high low. type = "vr" Vietoris-Rips filtration non-negative distance matrix. k-simplex \(\sigma\), filtration value \(\max_{(,j) \\sigma}\,d(,j)\). Thresholds run low high. Use max_scale cap filtration diameter.

title: Compare Subsequence Patterns Between Groups — sequence_compare
text: object class "net_sequence_comparison" containing: patterns Tidy data.frame, one row per retained k-gram pattern. Always present: pattern, length, one freq_<group>, prop_<group> resid_<group> column per group. test = "permutation": effect_size, p_value. test = "chisq": statistic, p_value. Rows ordered ascending adjusted p_value test run, descending maximum absolute residual otherwise. groups Character vector group names, sorted. n_patterns Integer. Number rows patterns, .e. patterns meeting min_freq every group. params List sub, min_freq, test, iter, adjust. print.net_sequence_comparison(): input object, invisibly. summary.net_sequence_comparison(): patterns data.frame: tidy, one row per k-gram pattern, frequency, proportion standardized-residual column per group, test columns test "none". plot.net_sequence_comparison(): drawn ggplot object, invisibly (plot also printed). NULL, invisibly, object holds patterns.

title: Compare Subsequence Patterns Between Groups — sequence_compare
text: Standardized residuals always computed 2xG contingency table (pattern vs. everything else) using textbook formula (o - e) / sqrt(e * (1 - r/N) * (1 - c/N)). describe much group's count given pattern deviates expectation independence, scaled approximately N(0,1) null. optional test argument chooses inference method: "permutation" Shuffles group labels across sequences recomputes per-pattern statistic (row-wise Euclidean residual norm). Answers: "pattern's distribution associated group membership actor level?" Respects sequence unit analysis; can underpowered number sequences small. "chisq" Runs chisq.test 2xG table per pattern. Answers: "group streams generate pattern different rates?" Treats k-gram occurrence event; fast powerful even sequences, iid assumption makes optimistic sequences strongly autocorrelated. "none" Skip inference. residuals, frequencies, proportions returned. P-values adjusted across patterns (per-pattern) using method supported p.adjust. default "fdr" (Benjamini-Hochberg).

title: Compare Subsequence Patterns Between Groups — sequence_compare
text: Visualizes pattern-level standardized residuals across groups. Two styles available, style = "auto" (default) picks number groups: "pyramid" Back--back bars pattern proportions, shaded side's standardized residual. Requires exactly 2 groups; explicit style = "pyramid" number error. "heatmap" One tile per (pattern, group) cell, colored standardized residual. Works number groups. Residuals read directly resid_<group> columns $patterns, always populated regardless inference method chosen sequence_compare.

title: Compare Subsequence Patterns Between Groups — sequence_compare
text: Haberman, S. J. (1973). analysis residuals cross-classified tables. Biometrics, 29(1), 205–220. (standardized residuals) Benjamini, Y. & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling false discovery rate. Journal Royal Statistical Society B, 57(1), 289–300. (default adjust = "fdr")

title: Compare Subsequence Patterns Between Groups — sequence_compare
code: set.seed(1) seqs <- data.frame(   V1 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 60, TRUE),   V2 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 60, TRUE),   V3 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 60, TRUE),   V4 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 60, TRUE) ) grp <- rep(c("X", "Y"), 30) net <- build_network(seqs, method = "relative") res <- sequence_compare(net, group = grp, sub = 2:3, test = "chisq")

what: Transition Entropy of a Markov Chain — transition_entropy
title: Transition Entropy of a Markov Chain — transition_entropy
text: Computes per-state branching entropy, stationary entropy, chain-level entropy rate Markov transition process. entropy rate \(H = -\sum_i \pi_i \sum_j P_{ij} \log_b P_{ij}\) (\(\pi\) stationary distribution eigendecomposition \(P^\top\) \(\lambda = 1\)) Shannon-McMillan-Breiman per-step uncertainty trajectories - canonical information-theoretic summary transition matrix, introduced behavioral research gaze transition entropy Krejtz et al. (2015) tracked real time mobile transition matrix entropy Krejtz et al. (2025). normalized fields (*_norm, division \(\log_b n\)) scale-free variants papers report.

title: Transition Entropy of a Markov Chain — transition_entropy
text: object class "net_transition_entropy" : row_entropy Named numeric vector, length \(n\). Per-state branching entropy \(H(P_{\cdot}) = -\sum_j P_{ij} \log P_{ij}\). row_entropy_norm Named numeric vector. row_entropy divided ceiling \(\log_b n\) (\([0, 1]\); zeros \(n = 1\)). stationary Named numeric vector. Stationary distribution \(\pi\). stationary_entropy Scalar. \(H(\pi) = -\sum_i \pi_i \log \pi_i\) - entropy \(\pi\) treated ..d. distribution. Upper bound entropy rate. stationary_entropy_norm Scalar. stationary_entropy divided ceiling \(\log_b n\). entropy_rate Scalar. \(h(P) = \sum_i \pi_i H(P_{\cdot})\) - Shannon-McMillan-Breiman entropy rate. entropy_rate_norm Scalar. entropy_rate divided ceiling \(\log_b n\). redundancy Scalar. \(H(\pi) - h(P)\), entropy deficit attributable serial dependence; zero ..d. chain (rows \(P\) equal \(\pi\)). redundancy_norm Scalar. relative redundancy \((H(\pi) - h(P)) / H(\pi)\) (fraction stationary entropy removed order-1 memory), redundancy divided \(\log_b n\); 0 \(H(\pi) = 0\). max_entropy Scalar. normalising ceiling \(\log_b n\). base Logarithm base used. states Character vector state names. netobject_group result "net_transition_entropy_group": named list holding one object per group. print.net_transition_entropy(), print.net_transition_entropy_group() print.summary.net_transition_entropy(): x invisibly. summary.net_transition_entropy(): summary.net_transition_entropy containing table tidy per-state data.frame, sorted contribution_pct descending chain tidy chain-level data.frame raw normalised \(h(P)\), \(H(\pi)\), redundancy, ceiling base logarithm base used plot.net_transition_entropy(): ggplot object.

title: Transition Entropy of a Markov Chain — transition_entropy
text: Convention \(0 \log 0 := 0\) applied, absorbing deterministic rows contribute zero per-row entropy. chain need irreducible; \(\pi\) computed eigendecomposition \(P^\top\) elsewhere package. non-ergodic chains returned \(\pi\) one stationary distribution among many - interpret help chain_structure. relation \(h(P) \leq H(\pi)\) holds equality iff successive states independent. deficit \(H(\pi) - h(P)\) reported redundancy - measure much memory chain order 1.

Bar widths proportional stationary probability visual area sums entropy rate. summary.net_transition_entropy(): Returns tidy per-state contribution table sorted share chain-level entropy rate (largest first), dominant contributors \(h(P)\) visible glance. row contains stationary mass, raw normalised row entropy, additive contribution \(\pi_i H(P_{\cdot})\), contribution percentage \(h(P)\).

what: Vertex Bootstrap for Network-Level Statistics — vertex_bootstrap
title: Vertex Bootstrap for Network-Level Statistics — vertex_bootstrap
text: Non-parametric vertex bootstrap single observed network (Snijders & Borgatti 1999). Vertices resampled replacement weight matrix rebuilt original entries resampled vertex pairs; network-level statistics computed replicate give bootstrap distributions, standard errors, confidence intervals. Unlike bootstrap_network, resamples underlying cases (sequences rows) therefore requires raw data stored netobject, vertex bootstrap needs weight matrix. works netobject - including data-less ones build_mlvar constituents as_tna(mcml) elements - plain weight matrices. two procedures answer different questions: case bootstrap quantifies sampling--subjects uncertainty edge weights; vertex bootstrap quantifies structural uncertainty whole-network descriptives given one network observed.

title: Vertex Bootstrap for Network-Level Statistics — vertex_bootstrap
text: replicate draws n vertex indices replacement sets W_b[, j] = W[idx_i, idx_j]. original vertex drawn two different positions, -diagonal cell structural self-pair; following Snijders & Borgatti, cells filled weight randomly chosen pair distinct original vertices. Diagonal entries carry original self-weight resampled vertex (W[idx_i, idx_i]) - self-loops meaningful transition networks never altered. undirected networks substitution applied symmetrically replicates stay symmetric. Built-statistics (computed -diagonal part weight matrix): density Proportion non-zero -diagonal cells. mean_weight Mean non-zero -diagonal weights. centralization Freeman-type strength centralization: sum(max(s) - s) / ((n - 1) * max(s)) s total node strength absolute weights. 0 nodes equal strength, approaching 1 star. reciprocity Directed networks . Weighted reciprocity sum(pmin(|W|, |t(W)|)) / sum(|W|) -diagonal cells: proportion total weight reciprocated.

title: Window-based Transition Network Analysis — wtna
text: Computes networks one-hot (binary indicator) data using temporal windowing. Supports transition (directed), co-occurrence (undirected), network types.

title: Window-based Transition Network Analysis — wtna
code: wtna(   data,   method = c("transition", "cooccurrence", "both"),   type = c("frequency", "relative"),   codes = NULL,   window_size = 3L,   mode = c("non-overlapping", "overlapping"),   actor = NULL )  # S3 method for class 'wtna_mixed' print(x, ...)

title: Window-based Transition Network Analysis — wtna
text: data Data frame one-hot encoded columns (0/1 binary). method Character. Network type: "transition" (directed), "cooccurrence" (undirected), "" (returns list two networks). Default: "transition". type Character. Output type: "frequency" (raw counts) "relative" (row-normalized probabilities). Default: "frequency". Note type = "relative" applied method = "cooccurrence" produces asymmetric matrix (conditional co-occurrence given row state), symmetric undirected weight matrix - use type = "frequency" symmetric co-occurrence counts required. codes Character vector NULL. Names one-hot columns use. NULL, auto-detects binary columns. Default: NULL. window_size Integer (>= 1). Number consecutive rows aggregate per window. Default: 3 (windowed pairwise -window counting). Set window_size = 1 ordinary consecutive (t -> t+1) transitions windowing. mode Character. Window mode: "non-overlapping" (fixed, separate windows) "overlapping" (rolling, step = 1). Default: "non-overlapping". actor Character NULL. Name actor/ID column per-group computation. NULL, treats rows one group. Default: NULL. x print() method: object class wtna_mixed. ... print.wtna_mixed(): Additional arguments (ignored).

title: Window-based Transition Network Analysis — wtna
text: method = "transition" "cooccurrence": c("netobject", "cograph_network") object (see build_network) method set "wtna_transition" "wtna_cooccurrence", directed = TRUE transitions, windowing settings (type, window_size, mode, codes, actor) recorded $params. Transition networks also carry $initial, per-actor-averaged initial state distribution. method = "": wtna_mixed object - list elements $transition $cooccurrence (netobject ) $method = "wtna_both". print.wtna_mixed(): input object, invisibly.

title: Window-based Transition Network Analysis — wtna
text: Transitions: Uses crossprod(X[-n,], X[-1,]) count often state active time t state j time t+1. Co-occurrence: Uses crossprod(X) count states simultaneously active row. Windowing: window_size > 1, rows aggregated windows computing networks. Non-overlapping windows fixed, separate blocks; overlapping windows roll forward one row time. Within window, active indicator (1) row makes state active window. Per-actor: actor specified, networks computed per group summed.

title: Window-based Transition Network Analysis — wtna
code: oh <- matrix(c(1,0,0, 0,1,0, 0,0,1, 1,0,0), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE,              dimnames = list(NULL, c("A","B","C"))) w <- wtna(oh)  # \donttest{ # Simple one-hot data df <- data.frame(   A = c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1),   B = c(0, 1, 0, 1, 0),   C = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 0) )  # Transition network net <- wtna(df) print(net) #> Network (method: wtna_transition) [directed] #>   Weights: [1.000, 2.000]  |  mean: 1.333 #>  #>   Weight matrix: #>     A B C #>   A 2 2 0 #>   B 1 1 0 #>   C 1 1 0  #>  #>   Initial probabilities: #>   A             1.000  ████████████████████████████████████████ #>   B             0.000   #>   C             0.000    # Both networks nets <- wtna(df, method = "both") print(nets$transition) #> Network (method: wtna_transition) [directed] #>   Weights: [1.000, 2.000]  |  mean: 1.333 #>  #>   Weight matrix: #>     A B C #>   A 2 2 0 #>   B 1 1 0 #>   C 1 1 0  #>  #>   Initial probabilities: #>   A             1.000  ████████████████████████████████████████ #>   B             0.000   #>   C             0.000   print(nets$cooccurrence) #> Network (method: wtna_cooccurrence) [undirected] #>   Weights: [1.000, 5.000]  |  mean: 2.333 #>  #>   Weight matrix: #>     A B C #>   A 5 3 2 #>   B 3 2 1 #>   C 2 1 1   # With windowing net <- wtna(df, window_size = 2, mode = "non-overlapping") # }
